items.q: Fill up: Besides electric shock, seizures, alcohol/cocaine/heroin, statins/zidovudine, hypothyroidism and polymyositis/dermatomyositis, the two electrolyte causes of rhabdomyolysis listed are ______ and hypophosphatemia.
items.exp: Causes of rhabdomyolysis include decreased K+ and decreased PO4(3-); hyperkalemia is a consequence of rhabdomyolysis, not a cause. The list also includes glycogen storage disease type 5 (McArdle disease), hypothyroidism and polymyositis/dermatomyositis. (Book p802)

items.q: Fill up: Glycogen storage disease type 5, also called ______ disease, is a listed cause of rhabdomyolysis.
items.exp: Glycogen storage disease type 5 (McArdle disease) is a listed cause, along with hypothyroidism and polymyositis/dermatomyositis. (Book p802)

items.q: All but one of the following are listed causes of rhabdomyolysis. Which is the odd one out?
items.exp: The list includes ↓K⁺/↓PO₄³⁻ (hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia) as a cause; hyperkalemia is a consequence, not a cause. (Book p802)

items.q: Match the pathophysiology of rhabdomyolysis — 1) Tubular effect  2) Vascular effect  3) Obstructive effect … A) Cast formation decreasing tubular flow  B) Hypovolemia and decreased renal perfusion  C) Direct toxicity of myoglobin in tubular cells
items.exp: Rhabdomyolysis pathophysiology: PCT injury + vasoconstriction + tubular obstruction with uric acid; the diagram shows direct myoglobin toxicity, cast formation decreasing tubular flow, and hypovolemia with decreased renal perfusion — all leading to AKI. (Book p802)

items.q: A young man with a crush injury has CK of 20,000 U/L and a creatinine that continues to rise beyond day 5. According to the note this suggests:
items.exp: CPK assay: >1500 units, rising after 2–12 hrs, peaking in 1–3 days, falling in 3–5 days — if there is no fall, suspect compartment syndrome. (Book p802)

items.q: The CPK level described as significant in rhabdomyolysis is:
items.exp: CPK assay >1500 units rises after 2–12 hrs, peaks in 1–3 days and falls in 3–5 days. (Book p802)

items.q: Match the rhabdomyolysis clinical features — 1) Muscles  2) Urine colour  3) Renal failure type  4) Urine sediment … A) Pigmented granular casts  B) Non-oliguric AKI (pre-renal failure)  C) Proximal muscle swelling  D) Upper/lower-limb muscle cramps with high coloured urine
items.exp: Clinical features: upper/lower-limb muscle cramps with high coloured urine (2); proximal muscle swelling (4); non-oliguric AKI — pre-renal failure (3); urine shows pigmented granular casts (1). (Book p802)

items.q: All but one of the following investigations are raised in rhabdomyolysis. Which is the odd one out?
items.exp: Investigations in rhabdomyolysis: ↑S.K⁺, ↑S.PO₄³⁻, ↑S.mg²⁺ and ↑S. uric acid, with ↓S.Ca²⁺, acidosis (HAGMA) and FeNa <1. (Book p802)

items.q: Match the urine findings in rhabdomyolysis — 1) Benzidine test  2) Urine microscopy  3) FeNa … A) Pigmented granular brown casts and renal tubular epithelial cell casts, with no RBCs  B) Positive (3+) for blood  C) Less than 1
items.exp: In rhabdomyolysis the benzidine (dipstick) test is 3+ positive for blood while urine microscopy shows no RBCs but pigmented granular brown casts and renal tubular epithelial cell casts; FeNa is <1. (Book p802)

items.q: Urine dipstick is positive for blood in a patient with rhabdomyolysis, but microscopy shows no RBCs. The explanation is:
opts: Myoglobin reacts with the benzidine (dipstick) test for blood but is not a red cell
The patient has a urinary tract infection
RBCs have all been lysed by alkaline urine
items.exp: Benzidine test 3+ with no RBC on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria; casts seen are pigmented granular brown casts and renal tubular epithelial casts. (Book p802)

items.q: The treatment of rhabdomyolysis consists of:
opts: Vigorous and intense hydration, alkalinization of urine and hemodialysis
Fluid restriction with diuretics and early high-dose corticosteroid therapy
Steroids with cyclophosphamide followed by a course of plasma exchange
IV rasburicase with allopurinol and hydration of 5–6 litres per day
items.exp: Treatment of rhabdomyolysis: vigorous & intense hydration, alkalinization of urine and hemodialysis. (Book p802)

items.q: The acidosis of rhabdomyolysis is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA), unlike the NAGMA of ATN.
opts: False — rhabdomyolysis does not alter acid-base status
items.exp: Investigations in rhabdomyolysis: acidosis (HAGMA) with FeNa <1; the ATN complication list specifies acidosis (NAGMA). (Book p802)

items.q: All but one of the following belong to the rhabdomyolysis picture. Which is the odd one out?
items.exp: Rhabdomyolysis has FeNa <1 (pre-renal component predominant), non-oliguric AKI and pigmented granular brown casts. (Book p802)
